item.title: Hyuga Natsu Citrus — Guide
item.description: Hyuga-natsu is a beautiful golden-yellow citrus fruit that is a speciality of Miyazaki (historically Hyuga province), grown in the sunny prefecture and prized for its refreshing flavour and fragrance. Roughly the size of a small grapefruit with a smooth, pale yellow rind, it has a uniquely delicate, sweet-tart, aromatic taste. What makes it special is the traditional way of eating it: unlike most citrus, the fluffy white pith (the spongy layer under the peel) is not discarded but eaten together with the juicy flesh, as it’s sweet and pleasant — the fruit is peeled thinly like an apple to leave the white layer on, then sliced.

item.title: Oita Kabosu Citrus — Guide
item.description: Kabosu is Oita’s signature citrus fruit, and the prefecture grows the overwhelming majority of Japan’s entire crop. A round, green citrus resembling a large lime, kabosu is prized not for eating whole but for its fragrant, tangy juice, which is squeezed over food much like a lemon or lime but with its own distinctive, refreshing aroma and a milder, more rounded acidity. In Oita it’s a beloved everyday condiment: a squeeze of kabosu brightens grilled fish and sashimi, the region’s famous Seki-saba and Seki-aji, Bungo beef, toriten, hotpots, noodles and even miso soup, and it’s used in ponzu, dressings, drinks, sweets and more.

item.title: Oita Shiitake Mushrooms — Guide
item.description: Oita is Japan’s foremost producer of dried shiitake mushrooms, and its high-quality log-grown shiitake are a signature product of the prefecture, prized across the country. In Oita’s forested, mountainous interior, shiitake are traditionally cultivated the natural way — grown on logs of kunugi (sawtooth oak) left in the cool, humid forest, a slow method that produces mushrooms of superior flavour and texture. The most prized grade, thick-capped ‘donko’ mushrooms harvested in cold weather, are especially valued.

item.title: Gunma Konnyaku: Japan's Konjac Capital — Guide
item.description: Gunma produces roughly 90% of Japan’s konjac (konnyaku), a low-calorie, high-fibre food made from the corm of the konjac plant, which thrives in the prefecture’s well-drained volcanic soil and cool climate. The gelatinous, jelly-textured food appears across Japanese cuisine in countless forms — firm grey blocks used in oden and simmered dishes, thread-like shirataki noodles, and even novelty sweets — and Gunma’s dedicated konnyaku shops and the themed Konnyaku Park near Fujioka let visitors sample the full range for free.

item.title: Ibaraki Chestnuts: Japan's Top Chestnut-Producing Prefecture — Guide
item.description: Ibaraki produces more chestnuts (kuri) than any other prefecture in Japan, its mild climate and well-drained soil ideal for cultivating large, sweet varieties prized by chefs and confectioners nationwide. Each autumn harvest, roadside stalls and farm shops sell fresh chestnuts alongside roasted snacks, while patisseries and traditional wagashi confectioners across the prefecture transform the harvest into monts blancs, chestnut cakes, sweetened kuri kinton and other refined seasonal treats. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Ibaraki Hours Peak season roughly September–November Admission Chestnuts and snacks from ~¥300–1,000 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Late September–October (peak harvest) What to Try Fresh roasted chestnuts, a classic autumn street snack.
